newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock crackdown sparks outcry from markets.
newsitem.headline: China stock crackdown sparks outcry from markets.

text.p: A sudden crackdown on China's fledgling stock markets pushed most shares to limit-down levels on Monday and triggered an outcry from securities brokerages and retail investors.

The People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Communist Party, said in a commentary on Monday the country's stock markets had overheated on speculation and warned that Beijing would not step in if the markets plunged. Virtually all shares on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets fell 10 percent, the daily limit announced by the authorities last Friday afternoon to prevent sharp fluctuations.
"This is very, very disappointing and outrageous," said a stock analyst. "With this simple decision they can wipe out nearly all the gains in the securities business in a hard year."
"I can't understand it," said a trader. "Such administrative edicts will eventually kill the markets one day."
Analysts were shocked by the change of direction by Beijing.
Since April there have been many official statements and hints indicating clearly that the stock markets had been given the official blessing of Beijing.
Domestic A shares have been rising since April as a result and B shares began a similar run in mid-November.

"They had been talking about encouraging stock invesment and suddenly here comes the new policy," said a retail investor. "Most of us will have our money caught in the markets. It looks like prices will plunge and no one wants to buy."
Foreign brokers and analysts slammed the official intervention, saying it went counter to the trend of gradually allowing market forces and controls to play a greater role.

"Foreign investors will not welcome such administrative interference in the markets," said a Shanghai-based brokerage analyst. "What is worse is that it seems from the People's Daily editorial that they wanted to force prices down."

In the morning session, Shanghai's domestic A share index plunged 9.95 percent to 1047.338 points and the foreign currency B shares fell 9.24 percent to 60.166 points. In Shenzhen in the morning session, the B index dived 9.89 percent to 134.58.
Brokers said virtually no buyers were in sight, indicating the indices would continue to free-fall in the short term.

"Panic selling occurred in many securities trading halls in major brokerages," said one trader. "But nobody wants to buy. Investors believe current prices are very high taking into account the changed market fundamentals after the crackdown."
"Market confidence was totally destroyed," said a second trader. "We can see no support for the time being. The B index is likely to head for a historical low at around 45 points shortly."
In Shenzhen, brokers said most Shenzhen-listed stocks were likely to register limit-down closes over the next few sessions as investors were intimidated by the People's Daily commentary.

An analyst with a major Chinese brokerage, commenting on the People's Daily description of recent stock market movements as "very abnormal and irrational", said: "To cool sentiment with such commentary is abnormal and irrational."

"They could have adopted other measures such as an effective ban on widespread illicit trading by institutional punters to cap share prices," a Shenzhen trader complained. "Instead, this method sacrifices many innocent small investors."
Many investors, including institutions, are sitting on heavy losses after the morning's crash and investor confidence is unlikely to recover over the short term, brokers said.

China's foreign currency B share market in Shanghai soared by about 80 percent between November 11 and December 10 while the bourse in the southern boomtown of Shenzhen rose by about 100 percent before sharp falls in the final days of last week.
Shanghai's A share index surged more than 100 percent and Shenzhen's A share index nearly 300 percent before the crackdown.
